---
title: "How to predict brain regions"
---

The region decoder assigns each recording channel a brain region from its
electrophysiological features. This guide runs it and reads the output correctly.

If you have not loaded a model yet, start with
[how to download a published model](download-models.qmd).

## What the model needs

```python
from ephysatlas import load_pretrained

model = load_pretrained(
    "int-brain-lab/ea-decoder-channel-xgboost", revision="2026_W42"
)

print(model.index["inputs"]["table"])   # raw_ephys_features_denoised.pqt
print(model.inputs["index"])            # ['pid', 'channel']
print(len(model.inputs["features"]))    # 48
print(model.config["region_map"])       # Cosmos
print(model.config["accuracy"])         # 0.6124
```

Three requirements, all of them enforced:

1. A DataFrame indexed by **`(pid, channel)`**.
2. Every column in `model.inputs["features"]`, by name. `predict` raises `KeyError`
   naming any that are absent.
3. Features that are **aggregated and denoised** for this model's vintage — see
   [aggregate and denoise](aggregate-and-denoise.qmd). This is not enforced, because it
   cannot be: a raw single-snippet table has the right column names and the wrong units.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The units trap

Denoising transforms some features — `rms_ap` and `rms_lf` to dB, `spike_count` (a rate,
in spikes/s) to log2 — and returns them transformed. A model trained on denoised features expects dB. Passing raw
volts produces no error and bad regions.
:::

## Predict

::: {.callout-warning}
## `raw_ephys_features_denoised.pqt` alone is not enough

It carries 47 of the 48 required columns. The missing one is **`outside`**, a boolean
derived from `channel_labels == 3` that is computed at read time rather than stored.
Passing the denoised table straight to `predict` raises:

```text
KeyError: 1 feature(s) required by this model are missing from the input
DataFrame: ['outside']. Expected all of: [...]
```

Verified against the published `ea_active/2026_W42` aggregate, and against a table
computed locally with
[`compute_denoised_features`](compute-features-spikeglx.qmd#many-snippets-from-one-recording).
:::

Three ways to get a complete table. On vintages from `2025_W39` on, the simplest is the
pre-merged file, which already contains `outside`:

```python
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

path_features = Path("/data/features/aggregated")   # or a downloaded vintage

df = pd.read_parquet(path_features / "df_all_cols_merged.pqt")
out = model.predict(df)

print(out[["predicted_acronym", "prediction_probability", "fold_agreement"]].head())
```

Or let `read_features_from_disk` derive it:

```python
import ephysatlas.data, ephysatlas.anatomy

df = ephysatlas.data.read_features_from_disk(
    path_features, brain_atlas=ephysatlas.anatomy.ClassifierAtlas()
)
out = model.predict(df)
```

Or derive it yourself — one line, and no atlas download:

```python
df = pd.read_parquet(path_features / "raw_ephys_features_denoised.pqt")
df["outside"] = df["channel_labels"] == 3
out = model.predict(df)
```

All three work. `out` is indexed exactly like `df`, one row per channel.

A real run on one probe of `ea_active/2026_W42` (`00a824c0-e060-495f-9ebc-79c82fef4c67`,
384 channels):

```text
predicted_acronym
MB            197
Isocortex     138
void           28
HPF            13
void_fluid      8

mean prob 0.779   mean fold_agreement 0.930
```

To try it with no data of your own, use the example the model ships:

```python
sample = model.path_model / "example" / "features_sample.parquet"
out = model.predict(pd.read_parquet(sample))
```

## Reading the output

| column | meaning |
|---|---|
| `predicted_acronym` | Winning region as an Allen acronym |
| `predicted_atlas_id` | The same region as a numeric Allen structure id |
| `prediction_probability` | Fold-averaged probability of the winning class |
| `fold_agreement` | Fraction of fold models that voted for the winner |
| `p_<acronym>` | One column per class, fold-averaged probability |

The `2026_W42` model predicts 13 **Cosmos**-level classes:

```python
print(model.config["class_acronyms"])
# ['void', 'MB', 'Isocortex', 'CB', 'TH', 'CNU', 'OLF', 'CTXsp', 'root', 'HB',
#  'HPF', 'HY', 'void_fluid']
```

Note that `void` and `void_fluid` are real classes: the model can say a channel is outside
brain tissue, which is useful for finding where a probe entered and exited.

### Two different kinds of uncertainty

`prediction_probability` and `fold_agreement` answer different questions, and reading only
the first will mislead you:

| probability | agreement | interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| high | high | Confident and consistent — trust it |
| low | high | Every fold agrees this channel is ambiguous, likely a region boundary |
| low | low | The folds disagree; the model has no coherent answer here |
| high | low | Rare and suspicious — inspect the channel |

```python
# Keep only channels the ensemble agrees on
confident = out[(out["prediction_probability"] > 0.5) & (out["fold_agreement"] >= 0.8)]
print(f"{len(confident)} / {len(out)} channels confidently assigned")
```

The published accuracy is around 0.60 across 13 classes, so filtering on these two columns
is not optional polish — it is how you use the output responsibly.

### The full probability distribution

The `p_<acronym>` columns give the whole posterior, not just the winner:

```python
prob_cols = [c for c in out.columns if c.startswith("p_")]
print(out[prob_cols].head())

# Runner-up per channel — often the anatomically adjacent region
top2 = out[prob_cols].apply(
    lambda r: r.nlargest(2).index[1].removeprefix("p_"), axis=1
)
```

## Ensemble or global

The release ships five cross-validation fold models plus one model trained on all
channels. `estimator=` picks between them:

```python
out = model.predict(df, estimator="ensemble")   # default
out = model.predict(df, estimator="global")
```

| | `"ensemble"` (default) | `"global"` |
|---|---|---|
| Weights | Averages the 5 fold models | The single all-data model |
| Cost | 5 forward passes | 1 forward pass |
| Calibration | Slightly better | Slightly worse |
| `fold_agreement` | Real value in [0, 1] | `NaN` |

`fold_agreement` is `NaN` for `global` on purpose: a single model has nothing to agree
with, and returning `1.0` would falsely imply unanimity among folds that were never
consulted.

::: {.callout-important}
The two estimators disagree on a small fraction of channels (3.9 % on the probe above).
Never mix them within one analysis — pick one and use it throughout.
:::

## Whole-probe decoder

A second region decoder reads a **whole probe at once**. `ProbeTransformerClassifier`
attends across all channels of a probe, using depth along the probe as its positional
signal. The XGBoost decoder above sees each channel independently.

```python
transformer = load_pretrained(
    "int-brain-lab/ea-decoder-channel-transformer", revision="2026_W42"
)

print(len(transformer.inputs["features"]))       # 51
print(transformer.inputs["position_column"])     # axial_um
print(transformer.config["region_map"])          # Cosmos

out_t = transformer.predict(df)
print(out_t[["predicted_acronym", "prediction_probability", "seed_agreement"]].head())
```

It takes the same denoised table, `outside` included, plus `axial_um`. Its inputs add the
four spike-shape columns (`spike_width_secs`, `predepolarisation_width_secs`,
`spike_amplitude`, `peak_to_trough_ratio_log`) to the XGBoost list, and drop
`channel_labels`. Two differences in the output:

- A release ships one model per random seed (five for `2026_W42`), so the agreement
  column is **`seed_agreement`**, not `fold_agreement`. `estimator="global"` uses the
  first seed alone and returns `seed_agreement` as `NaN`.
- Channels with any non-finite feature are dropped with a warning, so `out_t` can be a
  subset of `df`.

On the same probe, all 384 channels returned:

```text
predicted_acronym
MB            201
Isocortex     128
void           29
void_fluid     19
HPF             7

mean prob 0.816   mean seed_agreement 0.902
```

## Joining predictions onto your data

Prediction columns are namespaced so the join is always safe:

```python
joined = df.join(out)
```

Both the channel feature table and the cluster table already carry histology-derived
`acronym` and `atlas_id` columns. Bare output names would collide on join and silently
overwrite your ground truth on assignment. `predicted_acronym` / `predicted_atlas_id`
cannot.

That makes comparison against histology a one-liner:

```python
labelled = df.join(out)
match = labelled["predicted_acronym"] == labelled["acronym"]
print(f"agreement with histology: {match.mean():.1%}")
```

(Only meaningful when your `acronym` column is in the same region map — `Cosmos` for this
model. Remap first if it is not.)

## Denoising inside predict

If your table holds *raw* aggregated features, `predict` can denoise them for you:

```python
out = model.predict(df_raw, denoise=True)
```

Leave `denoise=False` (the default) when your features are already denoised. Denoising
twice degrades them.

Prefer denoising up front with
[`produce_output_dataframes`](aggregate-and-denoise.qmd): you get the denoised table on
disk for inspection, and you can reuse it across models.

## Plotting the result

`plot_cumulative_probas` draws the full posterior as stacked bands down the probe, in
Allen region colours:

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import ephysatlas.plots

# One probe at a time, sorted by depth
pid = df.index.get_level_values("pid")[0]
mask = df.index.get_level_values("pid") == pid
order = np.argsort(df.loc[mask, "axial_um"].to_numpy())

# The p_<acronym> columns are in class order, so they align with config["classes"]
prob_cols = [f"p_{a}" for a in model.config["class_acronyms"]]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3, 8))
ephysatlas.plots.plot_cumulative_probas(
    probas=out.loc[mask, prob_cols].to_numpy()[order],
    depths=df.loc[mask, "axial_um"].to_numpy()[order],
    aids=np.asarray(model.config["classes"]),   # one id per class, not per channel
    ax=ax,
    legend=True,
)
ax.set(xlabel="cumulative probability", ylabel="depth (µm)")
plt.show()
```

Two things to get right here: `aids` is one atlas id per **class** (13 of them), not one
per channel; and `ax` must be supplied — the function draws onto the axes you give it and
returns it.

See [plotting features along the probe](plot-features-along-probe.qmd) for the
depth-resolved feature view beside the predictions.

## Troubleshooting

**`KeyError` listing feature columns** — your table is missing those columns. Usually a
feature family you did not compute; the `2026_W42` model needs all four (`lf`, `csd`,
`ap`, `waveforms`), and `waveforms` needs the `[full]` extra. A list of
`peak_val`, `trough_val`, `peak_time_secs` and friends means the opposite mismatch: a
model older than `2026_W39` on a table from `ephysatlas` 0.9.0 or later, which no longer
has those columns. Use a `2026_W39` or later model. A list of `*_bpr` columns means a
`2026_W42` model on an older table read with `pd.read_parquet`; read it with
`read_features_from_disk`, which renames the `*_csd_diff1` columns, or better, use the
model of the table's own vintage.

**`ValueError` about the feature-order digest** — the manifest's feature list no longer
matches its recorded hash, meaning the model directory has been edited. Re-download it.

**Predictions look uniformly wrong** — check three things in order: `model.selftest()`
passes; your features are denoised; the feature vintage matches
`model.index["vintage"]`.

**Everything predicted `void` or `root`** — often a sign the input is raw rather than
denoised, so the feature values sit far outside the training distribution.

**`transformer.predict` never returns after the XGBoost decoder ran in the same process
(macOS)** — XGBoost and PyTorch each load their own OpenMP runtime, and the second one
deadlocks. Importing `torch` first instead crashes the XGBoost predict. Start Python with
`OMP_NUM_THREADS=1` (`OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 python my_script.py`), or run the two decoders in
separate processes. Seen with XGBoost 3.4.1 and PyTorch 2.14 on Apple Silicon.
